prize_parts.citation: For an inward, encyclopedic prose imagination in Romanian that turns memory, the body and dream into a sustained metaphysical project and renews the means of the novel.

statement.case_for: My opening view holds after reading the colleagues' opening files. The case for Cărtărescu rests on literary criteria, not on the fact that the opening rankings coincide. The longlist entry describes visionary, densely patterned prose that makes memory and the body the material of an expansive metaphysical project, with Blinding and Solenoid as representative works. On public knowledge, the voice is distinctive and the formal ambition is high: very long architectures built from recurring images, with the same imaginative scheme running through the prose and the poetry. The intellectual depth is sustained across volumes rather than concentrated in one book, and the later large works extend the early project instead of repeating it. That is the best fit with my criteria of voice, formal and linguistic achievement, sustained quality and significance across a body of work. Prose of this kind, in which a language is made to carry a private cosmology, is the part of the longlist where I find the idiom most singular. I put Carson and Adonis next on the same criteria. Carson renews genre boundaries through classical learning; Adonis remade a poetic language through a long dialogue with inherited forms.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is translation and corpus coverage. Whether the prose texture, syntactic control and long-breath rhythm that make the case really sustain a work of this length cannot be assessed by me independently of translation, and I have not independently read or verified the Romanian originals. The early poetry and essays are less accessible than the novels, so the corpus is covered unevenly. The maximalist scale may also hide unevenness or excess over very long works, and I cannot rule that out from public knowledge. There is a further open question about how an encyclopedic, inward and often disturbing imaginative project fits the will's reference to work of an idealistic tendency; that is a matter of interpretation, and I do not treat it as settled in either direction.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first on the coherence and scale of the oeuvre, and asks of Carson whether her achievement is sustained across many volumes or concentrated in a few landmark books such as Autobiography of Red and Nox.
responses.response: I agree that the question about Carson is the central one, and it is the main reason I keep her as an alternative rather than as my first choice. Her voice is unmistakable and the formal invention is real, but the Nobel framework asks about the whole oeuvre, and I cannot say whether the shorter and occasional pieces and the translations carry the weight that the two best-known books do. I share her reservation about how to treat the classical translations and scholarship, which are a separate strand. I would add that coherence and scale are not enough by themselves. For Cărtărescu the question is also whether the later volumes deepen the early project, and I read the public record as showing development, though I cannot verify it independently.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Murnane second for a rigorous, inward fiction whose formal radicalism comes from restraint, but she acknowledges that its narrow thematic range may limit the claim to wide significance. She ranks Carson only sixth, citing doubt about whether the later work consolidates or restates the early breakthroughs.
responses.response: I take the formal case for Murnane seriously: the austere, self-scrutinizing method of The Plains and Border Districts is distinctive, and consistency is a strength for sustained quality. I ranked him fourth because I share her concern about breadth. A deliberately narrow range is a legitimate artistic choice, but significance across a body of work is one of the criteria, and his strength is intensity rather than extension. On Carson I am more positive than she is, though I accept the unresolved point about whether the later work develops the method or only repeats it, and I would want the committee to examine that directly before treating her as a first choice.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Adonis second for a major reshaping of Arabic poetic language, but notes that timing is delicate because of his advanced age and that the weight of the essays and public positions needs care.
responses.response: I agree that the essays and public positions must be kept separate from the literary judgment, and I would keep the case for Adonis on the poems and on the critical prose where it concerns poetic language. I would go further on the age point: it is not a literary criterion, and I would not let it count for or against him. The real difficulty is the one Sem-Sandberg also names, that Arabic prosody and the resonance of classical forms are the heart of the achievement and are the part that translation loses most. I rank him third because of that uncertainty about how well the committee can judge the work, not because I doubt the significance of the project.

responses.point: Sward ranks Yan Lianke second for grotesque and mythic fiction, supported by his poetics of mythorealism, and insists that the case must rest on narrative form rather than on political symbolism.
responses.response: I agree with the principle, and it is the standard I apply to every candidate: censorship and political context do not by themselves establish merit. On the form, the invention of a mythic and grotesque narrative mode in The Four Books and The Explosion Chronicles is a real contribution, and the oeuvre is large and still developing. My reservation is the one both of us record, namely that Chinese prose style is hard to judge through uneven translations, and that some titles appear stronger than others in the translated record. That is why I rank him fifth. I would need a clearer account of how consistent the quality is across the whole body of work before I could move him ahead of the poets.

responses.point: Palm ranks Alexis Wright second for polyphonic novels that renew the form through Indigenous oral traditions and ecological time, and acknowledges that the oeuvre is modest in size, so sustained achievement is harder to judge.
responses.response: The formal ambition of Carpentaria and The Swan Book is distinctive, and I agree that the case has to rest on form and language rather than on topical significance. I ranked her lower, eighth, mainly because of the point Palm herself raises: a small number of major novels makes it harder to assess quality over a long arc, which is the criterion I weigh most heavily after voice. I do not think that makes the work less important, and the nonfiction and recent work may change the picture, but I cannot confirm that from public knowledge. If the committee wanted to examine her case further, the first question would be how the later and nonfiction writing extends the two central novels.

uncertainties: My assessment of Cărtărescu's prose rests on public knowledge and translation reception, not on independent reading of the Romanian originals.
Translation coverage of the poetry, early work and essays is thinner than for the major novels, so the corpus is covered unevenly.
Whether the later very long works consistently deepen the early project, or are uneven over their length, cannot be verified here.
How the will's reference to work of an idealistic tendency applies to an inward, encyclopedic and often disturbing imaginative project is a matter of interpretation.
For the alternatives, Carson's sustained quality across many volumes and the weight of her translations, and the translatability of Adonis's Arabic poetry, remain unresolved.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My scholarly interests in modern poetry, the fragment and exile literature are context only and do not establish a preference for any candidate. The profile records no connection to any shortlisted writer.
